items.headline: AMD brings native ROCm support to vLLM's vime RL post-training framework
items.diff_narrative: A net-new topic with no 2026-07-12 antecedent. The vLLM project's vime reinforcement-learning post-training framework now runs end-to-end on AMD Instinct MI355X GPUs through native ROCm, shipped as a prebuilt Docker container that removes the from-source build long gating ROCm adoption. Published Qwen3-4B, Qwen3-8B, and Qwen3-30B-A3B runs report throughput near 4,100 tokens per GPU per second, training-versus-rollout log-probability divergence around 0.012, and reward climbing from roughly zero to about 0.5 to 0.6 by step 100. Where yesterday's hardware story was Micron's memory-capacity buildout, today's is a software one: reinforcement-learning post-training, until now almost entirely CUDA-bound, gains a working non-NVIDIA path, and it puts concrete substance behind the AMD Advancing AI keynote both days' event calendars flag.

items.headline: MemGhost plants persistent false memories in personal AI agents via one email
items.diff_narrative: This extends the AI-agent trust-boundary attack thread that GhostApproval opened on 2026-07-12, moving it onto a new surface. Where GhostApproval tricked coding assistants into redirecting a file write onto a victim's SSH keys through a repository symlink, MemGhost poisons a personal agent's long-term memory with a single crafted email: the agent writes attacker-chosen facts into its persistent memory, returns an innocuous reply that shows nothing happened, then lets those facts steer later, unrelated sessions. Both land on the same agent ecosystem, with Claude Code figuring in each, but the failure shifts from a consent bypass on a filesystem write to a stealthy persistence attack, measured here on the new 108-case WhisperBench and succeeding in 87.5% of background runs against OpenClaw on GPT-5.4 and 71.4% against a Claude Code SDK agent on Sonnet 4.6, transferring across architectures and memory backends. The thread advances from an agent being tricked into one bad write to agent memory as an unaudited persistence layer an outsider can write to.

items.headline: Orca Security's 2026 State of AI Security report finds 99.9% of fixable AI vulnerabilities unpatched
items.diff_narrative: A new topic with no 2026-07-12 precedent, where yesterday's slate was GhostApproval, a humanoid-robotics benchmark, and Micron's fab investment. Orca Security's 2026 State of AI Security report, drawn from live cloud-estate scans, finds 99.9% of AI vulnerability alerts that already have a fix still unpatched, 81.2% of organizations running AI packages carrying at least one known vulnerability and 74.1% at least one critical CVE, while 56% have pushed agent frameworks and 64% vector databases into production and nearly 30% store an AI API key insecurely. Rather than another single attack, it supplies the denominator beneath the week's disclosures: it quantifies how large, and how unpatched by default, the surface those techniques land on actually is.

items.headline: AI events roundup: AMD Advancing AI plus the summer-to-autumn summit calendar
items.diff_narrative: Carries yesterday's calendar forward largely intact, with AMD Advancing AI on July 22-23 remaining the nearest date, followed by Hot Chips (early rate closing July 31), the AI Infra Summit, Black Hat and DEF CON's AI Village, the Half Moon Bay AI Risk Summit, Anyscale's Ray Summit on August 24-26, Ai4, the ACM AI Leadership Summit, The AI Conference, GitHub Universe, AWS re:Invent, and NeurIPS. The substantive change is one fresh entry: World Summit AI brings its roughly 10,000-attendee flagship to Amsterdam's Taets Art & Event Park on October 7-8, extending the roundup into the European autumn circuit. The AMD Advancing AI framing also sharpens, now reading as a counterpoint to today's AMD-on-vLLM reinforcement-learning work rather than a generic answer to Blackwell.
